prompt: A server was down for an hour and nobody noticed until a customer called. Which of the five questions failed first?
hint: Not only whether it is up, but whether somebody would know.

choices.why: Nothing had to be restored; it was down, not lost.
Access was not the problem here.
A limit may have caused it, but the failure described is not noticing.
Right. Its answer includes knowing within minutes.

prompt: A team has nightly backups and has never restored one. How should the question "can it be restored?" be answered?

choices.text: Yes, there is a backup from last night
choices.why: A backup nobody restored is a hope, not evidence.

choices.text: Yes, if the backup tool reported success
choices.why: Success at writing is not success at restoring.

choices.text: It depends on the size of the database
choices.why: Size changes how long, not whether you know.

choices.text: Unknown, until one is restored and timed
choices.why: Right. Only having done it answers it.

prompt: Most outages that are not hardware failures share one property. Which?

choices.why: The time is not the pattern the lesson names.

choices.text: They come from bugs in PostgreSQL
choices.why: The lesson names limits, not bugs.
Schema changes cause some, not most.
Right. A disk, a connection limit, a table outgrowing its maintenance.

prompt: Match each question to the lessons that answer it.

pairs.left: How does the server change safely?

prompt: Which layer does the lesson say is shared between developer and administrator?

choices.why: Queries are above the line: the developer's.
Below the line: the administrator's.
The administrator's, told to the developer.
Right. One knows what the data means, the other what a change costs.

prompt: A query reads a million rows to show twenty. The administrator silently adds an index and it becomes fast. What is wrong?
hint: Who owns the query, and who was told?

choices.text: Nothing; a faster query is the goal
choices.why: The cause was in the application and is still there for the next query.

choices.text: Indexes are forbidden on large tables
choices.why: They are not; they have a cost, which is another matter.
Either may; the problem is doing it silently.

choices.text: The fix hides a developer's problem and nobody was told
choices.why: Right. Above the line, and the last column of the table.

prompt: Why is an unannounced restart of the database a problem even when it takes ten seconds?
hint: It lands on somebody else's half.

choices.why: A clean restart corrupts nothing.

choices.text: PostgreSQL forbids restarts during the day
choices.why: It forbids nothing of the kind.
Passwords live in the cluster and survive restarts.

choices.text: An application that does not reconnect breaks
choices.why: Right. The cost falls on the other side of the line.

prompt: Match each situation to who acts first.

pairs.left: A new feature needs a table
A new service needs read access

prompt: On the first day with an inherited server you find a setting that looks wrong. What do you do?

choices.text: Write it down, with how you found it
choices.why: Right. Changes come from the inventory, in order of risk.
It may be holding up something you have not found yet.

choices.text: Restart the server to see if it matters
choices.why: A restart to find out is a change with consequences.

choices.text: Ask the developers to remove it
choices.why: Server settings are below the line; and nothing is changed yet.

prompt: Why should an inventory say what is not known yet, such as "no restore on record"?
hint: What does a missing line let the next reader assume?

choices.text: It makes the document longer and more complete-looking
choices.why: Length is not the point.
The lesson's reason is the next person, not an audit.

choices.text: A missing line lets the next reader assume somebody checked
choices.why: Right. The gap is a finding.
The inventory is where the runbook starts.

prompt: Put the first day with an inherited server in order.
items: Write each answer down with its date and command
List what to change, by risk
trap: Changing before writing down loses the state you started from.

prompt: A server runs a major version past its end of life, and everything works. Why is that still the first finding to report?

choices.why: Right. The next vulnerability stays open.

choices.text: It will stop working on a fixed date
choices.why: It keeps working; that is why it gets left alone.
The version does not change growth.

choices.text: Clients refuse to connect to old versions
choices.why: Clients connect to old servers for years.

prompt: A server will not start. What is the first habit the lesson asks for?

choices.why: That changes things before knowing what is wrong.
A restore is the last resort, not the first look.
A restart without reading loses the evidence on screen.
Right. It says what is wrong more often than people expect.

prompt: Why does the course insist on a number before and after a change?

choices.why: Appearance is not the reason.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses changes without a benchmark
choices.why: It refuses nothing of the kind.
That may be true, but it is not the lesson's reason.

choices.text: Without them nobody knows whether the change helped
choices.why: Right. A guess with consequences, otherwise.

prompt: A colleague sets a parameter with SET in a session to fix a slow report, and it works. What is the problem a week later?

choices.why: Right. A setting in memory is not a setting anyone can find.

choices.text: SET changes the value for every session forever
choices.why: It lasts for that session only — which is the trouble.
Nothing forbids it.

choices.text: The value is written to postgresql.conf by itself
choices.why: SET writes nothing to any file.

prompt: Anything that cannot be undone in a minute is first ___ on a copy.
hint: As a play before opening night.

prompt: Which course owns backups and point-in-time recovery?

choices.why: That one owns making queries fast.
That one takes the questions to MongoDB, Redis and Cassandra.
Right.
That one teaches SQL and is assumed here.

prompt: From which lesson on does the course ask you to type commands, and on what machine?

choices.text: Lesson 1, on a server the platform provides
choices.why: The platform provides none.

choices.text: Lesson 3, on a VM of your own
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu and PostgreSQL 16.

choices.text: Lesson 5, once the configuration is explained
choices.why: Lesson 3 already installs the server.
Lesson 2's transcripts are for reading.

prompt: A developer asks you to raise max_connections because the application opens a connection per request. Using the lesson's line, what is the honest first answer?
hint: Whose side is the cause on?

choices.text: Talk about how the application connects
choices.why: Right. Cause above the line, consequence below it.

choices.text: Raise it; server settings are yours to change
choices.why: The setting is yours, but the cause is above the line; lesson 10 says why raising it is rarely the fix.

choices.text: Refuse; developers may not ask for settings
choices.why: They may ask; the lesson is about telling each other.

choices.text: Move the database to a managed service
choices.why: The same limit exists there.

prompt: Which of these are habits the lesson asks for? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Say what you are about to do
choices.why: Yes.
Yes.

choices.text: Tune settings until the server feels fast
choices.why: Feeling is not measuring.
Yes.

choices.text: Fix everything on the first day
choices.why: The first day is an inventory.
